How a bug in a Scottish racing game became the most profitable entertainment product ever made, why its maker spent thirteen years not building a sequel, and why the rest of the industry is clearing the road for November 19.

A video game released in September 2013, for consoles now two generations obsolete, has sold more than 230 million copies and grossed more money than any film, album or book in history, according to the analysts who track it. Its publisher's revenue has risen more than fivefold since. The sequel arrives on November 19 at $79.99, with no disc in the box and no multiplayer at launch, and it is already the strongest pre-order campaign anyone has measured.

Rockstar Games employs a few thousand people and works out of offices above a Manhattan street. Last autumn it fired staff who were organising a union, and the tribunal runs right up to launch. It spent this summer filing takedown notices against leaked footage of its own product. By any commercial measure it is also the most successful studio in the medium, and it has shipped two new games in eight years.

Rockstar decided early that it would rather be a record label than a software firm. It treated controversy as a distribution channel until the day a US Senator got involved, and it stumbled into a business model that turned a one-time purchase into a thirteen-year annuity. The story starts in a factory town on the east coast of Scotland.
